clinicalScope: Chronic hepatitis B infection in children and adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Hepatitis B Infection
subject: Medicine
summary: Hepatitis B is a viral infection that can damage the liver and cause long‑term illness. In East Africa it is common, often spread by unsafe injections or from mother to child, and many patients present without obvious symptoms.

sections.p: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a partially double‑stranded DNA virus that infects hepatocytes and can cause acute, chronic liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
b: Global prevalence ~260 million chronic carriers; highest endemicity in sub‑Saharan Africa.
In East Africa, chronic infection prevalence ranges 8‑12 % in the general population.
Vertical transmission accounts for >50 % of chronic cases in this region.
Adult‑to‑adult sexual transmission is the second most common route.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: Transmission pathways reflect local health‑system practices and cultural behaviours.
b: Perinatal exposure – infected mother, no birth‑dose vaccine.
Unsafe injections – re‑used needles in clinics, traditional scarification.
Unprotected sex – multiple partners, low condom use.
Co‑infection with HIV or malaria increases viral replication.
Traditional herbal remedies applied to skin breaches.

sections.p: HBV enters hepatocytes via the sodium‑taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor, deposits its relaxed circular DNA, and forms covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) that persists in the nucleus, driving chronic infection.
b: cccDNA acts as a stable template for viral mRNA → continuous antigen production.
Immune‑mediated hepatocyte injury causes ALT/AST rise and fibrosis.
High HBV DNA and HBeAg indicate active replication and greater transmission risk.
Integration of HBV DNA into host genome contributes to HCC risk.

sections.p: Clinical picture varies with age and phase of infection.
b: Infants: usually asymptomatic, high chance of chronicity.
Children 5‑15 y: mild fatigue, occasional right‑upper‑quadrant discomfort, normal exam.
Adults: jaundice, anorexia, nausea, dark urine, tender hepatomegaly; 30 % are asymptomatic.
Acute fulminant hepatitis: encephalopathy, coagulopathy (INR > 1.5).

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and exam quickly differentiate acute from chronic disease and identify complications.
b: Ask about birth‑dose vaccine, maternal HBV status, recent injections, sexual partners, and HIV status.
Enquire about alcohol use, herbal medicines, and prior liver disease.
Examine for jaundice, spider nevi, palmar erythema, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, and asterixis.
Check for signs of portal hypertension (caput medusae, variceal bleed).

sections.p: Other conditions that cause similar liver enzyme elevations or jaundice must be considered.
b: Acute hepatitis A or E – usually self‑limited, IgM anti‑HAV/E positive.
Alcoholic hepatitis – history of heavy drinking, AST : ALT ratio > 2.
Malaria‑related hepatopathy – recent febrile illness, positive rapid test.
Autoimmune hepatitis – ANA/ASMA positive, hypergammaglobulinemia.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: If HBV DNA testing is unavailable, treat based on HBeAg status, ALT elevation, and fibrosis assessment (e.g., APRI score).

t.b: Is there active infection? Positive = acute or chronic infection.
Is the patient immune? Positive = vaccination or resolved infection.
Is the infection recent (<6 months)? Positive = acute infection.
What is the viral load? >20 000 IU/mL in HBeAg‑negative or >2000 IU/mL in HBeAg‑positive guides treatment.
How much hepatocellular injury? ALT > 2 × ULN suggests active disease.
Is there synthetic dysfunction? INR > 1.5 signals decompensation.
Is there fibrosis, cirrhosis, or HCC? Look for coarse echotexture, nodules, splenomegaly.

sections.p: Staging combines serology, liver enzymes, and fibrosis assessment.
b: Phase 1 (immune‑tolerant): HBeAg +, high HBV DNA, normal ALT, minimal fibrosis.
Phase 2 (immune‑active): HBeAg +, elevated ALT, HBV DNA 20 000‑200 000 IU/mL, fibrosis may progress.
Phase 3 (inactive carrier): HBeAg‑, anti‑HBc IgG, HBV DNA < 2000 IU/mL, normal ALT.
Phase 4 (reactivation): HBeAg‑, ALT rise, HBV DNA > 2000 IU/mL.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities common in low‑resource settings alter disease course.
b: HIV co‑infection → higher HBV DNA, faster fibrosis.
Malaria or TB treatment (rifampicin) can reduce tenofovir levels.
Traditional herbal hepatotoxins increase risk of decompensation.
Pregnancy may accelerate viral replication; monitor closely.

sections.p: Therapy aims to suppress viral replication, prevent liver damage, and reduce transmission.
b: 1️⃣ Counsel on avoidance of alcohol, hepatotoxic drugs, and unsafe injections.
2️⃣ Initiate nucleos(t)ide analogue (tenofovir or entecavir) when: HBeAg‑positive with ALT > 2 × ULN, or HBV DNA > 20 000 IU/mL with fibrosis (APRI > 1.0).
3️⃣ Monitor ALT, HBV DNA, and renal function every 3‑6 months.
4️⃣ For selected HBeAg‑positive, low‑fibrosis patients, pegylated interferon‑α may be considered (avoid if decompensated).
5️⃣ Manage complications: diuretics for ascites, beta‑blockers for variceal bleed prophylaxis, surveillance ultrasound for HCC every 6 months.
Fulminant hepatitis: encephalopathy, INR > 1.5, bilirubin > 10 mg/dL → urgent transfer to higher‑level care.
Decompensated cirrhosis: ascites, variceal bleed, hepatic encephalopathy.
Hepatocellular carcinoma: new right‑upper‑quadrant mass, AFP > 200 ng/mL.
Renal dysfunction from tenofovir – monitor creatinine.
Infants (<1 y): give hepatitis B immunoglobulin + vaccine within 12 h of birth; monitor HBsAg at 9 months.
Pregnant women: screen at first antenatal visit; treat with tenofovir if HBV DNA > 200 000 IU/mL to reduce vertical transmission.
HIV‑positive patients: use tenofovir‑based ART that also suppresses HBV.
Patients with renal impairment: prefer entecavir (dose‑adjust) or monitor tenofovir trough levels.

sections.p: Long‑term outcomes depend on viral suppression and complication management.
b: Undetectable HBV DNA for ≥12 months predicts low risk of cirrhosis.
Annual ultrasound ± AFP for HCC surveillance in cirrhotic patients.
Vaccination of newborns (pentavalent series) and high‑risk adults reduces incidence.
Safe injection practices and blood‑screening are essential public‑health measures.

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls common in low‑resource labs.
b: Transient HBsAg positivity after recent vaccination – repeat after 4 weeks.
Low‑level HBV DNA may be missed by qualitative PCR; consider quantitative assay if suspicion high.
ALT can be normal in advanced fibrosis; use fibrosis scores (APRI, FibroScan if available).
Co‑infection with hepatitis D can suppress HBsAg, leading to false‑negative serology.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of confusion or coma (hepatic encephalopathy)
Severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen (possible hepatic rupture)
Bleeding from varices or melena with hypotension

faq.q: Can a person be immune without vaccination?
faq.a: Yes, recovery from past infection leaves anti‑HBs antibodies, indicating immunity.

faq.q: Why is tenofovir preferred over lamivudine?
faq.a: Tenofovir has higher potency and a much lower rate of viral resistance.
In low‑resource settings non‑invasive scores (APRI) are used; biopsy is reserved for ambiguous cases.

exam: What serologic pattern distinguishes acute HBV from chronic infection? — IgM anti‑HBc positive in acute; anti‑HBc IgG with HBsAg >6 months in chronic.

A 30‑year‑old man with HBsAg+, ALT 300 U/L, HBV DNA 1 × 10⁶ IU/mL, APRI 1.2. What is the next step? — Start tenofovir (or entecavir) because he meets treatment criteria (high DNA, elevated ALT, significant fibrosis).
Why is interferon‑α contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis? — It can worsen hepatic inflammation and precipitate liver failure.
How does HIV co‑infection alter HBV management? — Requires tenofovir‑based ART; monitor for higher HBV DNA and faster fibrosis.

Explain the rationale for giving hepatitis B immunoglobulin to a newborn of an HBsAg‑positive mother. — Provides passive immunity while the vaccine induces active immunity, reducing vertical transmission to <5 %.
What bedside sign suggests portal hypertension in chronic HBV? — Palpable spleen with splenomegaly and/or caput medusae.
A patient has normal ALT but APRI 1.5. How do you interpret? — ALT may be normal in advanced fibrosis; APRI indicates significant fibrosis, warranting treatment.
Which laboratory result would mislead you into thinking the patient is immune? — Anti‑HBs positive after recent vaccination without checking HBsAg; repeat testing needed.
Describe the pathophysiologic role of cccDNA in chronic HBV. — cccDNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei, serving as a template for continuous viral protein production, making cure difficult.
What are the red‑flag features of fulminant hepatitis B? — Encephalopathy, INR > 1.5, bilirubin > 10 mg/dL, rapid rise in transaminases.
